video_title: Sawdust to Paw Patrol: The Spin Master Story (with Ronnen Harary) 7/13/26
gist: Spin Master co-founder Ronnen Harary walks Russ Roberts through the operating logic that took a $1.65 sawdust-and-pantyhose novelty (Earth Buddy) to a $2.3B-revenue, #4-globally toy company: treat foreign fad data as a market-size arbitrage signal, accept that novelty products have a short half-life and stack narrative IP (Bakugan, Paw Patrol) on top of physical toys to escape it, and design products and companies to fail gracefully rather than never fail. The conversation is a consumer-products and IP-durability case study rather than a markets episode, with concrete unit economics, order sizes, and franchise-longevity mechanics throughout.

insights.claim: Ronnen Harary argues entrepreneurial risk assessment is systematically biased because downside scenarios are easy to enumerate while upside scenarios are unmodelable, so conventional pro/con analysis structurally under-prices new ventures.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: The same asymmetry applies to early-stage and venture underwriting: any process that scores enumerable downside against unenumerable upside will structurally reject convex bets.
insights.quote: It's really, really easy to game out the downside. It's very hard to game out the upside because you don't know what's going to actually happen.

insights.claim: Harary frames salaried employment as 'renting your time,' where all the upside accrues to the employer, and argues the correct comparison is total earnings amortized over a 20- to 30-year arc rather than income in the first ten years.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: A duration-matched framing of career choice: the equity-vs-wage tradeoff is a term-structure question, and short-horizon comparisons systematically favor employment.
insights.quote: essentially, you're renting your time, right? versus having that time acrew back to you

insights.claim: Harary claims passion functions as a risk-reduction mechanism ('passion delevers risk') and that ventures reasoned into intellectually, without genuine enthusiasm, do not work.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: A diligence heuristic: founder conviction is not soft signal but a substitute for experience, and purely opportunistic 'the market is big' theses are a negative screen.
insights.quote: passion delevers risk

insights.claim: Harary contends youth is an underpriced commercial asset because counterparties actively want inexperienced founders to succeed, citing a Kmart buyer who gave a 23-year-old an order for a product she could have sourced from seven established competitors.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Counter-consensus: inexperience can be a distribution advantage in relationship-driven B2B sales, not merely a discount factor.
insights.quote: One of the greatest assets you have when you're young is this. Everyone is rooting for you to win.

insights.claim: Harary argues the dominant cost of not starting a business is misallocated time rather than lost capital, because young people can recover from monetary losses but not from spent years.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Reframes the risk denominator from dollars to years, which inverts the standard risk ranking of safe employment versus founding.

insights.claim: Harary's original market-sizing for Earth Buddy came from summing the self-reported unit sales of six Israeli manufacturers profiled in a newspaper spread — roughly 300,000 units in a country of 10 million — and extrapolating that per-capita penetration to an untapped North American market.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: A repeatable scouting method: proven per-capita adoption in one geography plus zero competitive presence in a larger one is a quantifiable, low-cost arbitrage signal.
insights.quote: I added up all the six and it came to like 300,000 pieces in a country of 10 million

insights.claim: Spin Master's founding product had no proprietary technology — the concept originated in Turkey with no known inventor, and Harary and partner Anton Rabie reverse-engineered the recipe by sourcing pantyhose from Kmart plus sawdust and grass seed.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Illustrates that in consumer novelty, execution and distribution — not IP — are the moat, which is why these categories commoditize fast.

insights.claim: The Kmart deal turned on physically walking the corporate building after being told 'I'm not the buyer' three times, locating the horticulture buyer unannounced, and waiting five hours in the lobby rather than leaving for lunch.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Category placement was non-obvious — a toy sold through the garden department — a reminder that channel/category fit can be the binding constraint in retail distribution.
insights.quote: I'm not the buyer for this product.

insights.claim: Harary cut his Earth Buddy ask from $2.60 to $1.65 US against roughly $0.70 US cost after seeing seven competing grass-head products on the buyer's shelf, and later concluded he left 50–70 cents per unit on the table across an order that reached 1.5 million units.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Quantifies the cost of pricing to visible competition rather than to buyer intent — roughly $750K–$1M of foregone gross margin on a single account.
insights.quote: I probably sold it too cheap. giving away maybe 50 to 70 cents per EarthBuddy.

insights.claim: The Kmart buyer opened with a firm 48,000-unit order and a conditional commitment of half a million units for Christmas, and Kmart ultimately sold 1.5 million Earth Buddies at $4.99 retail against a $1.65 wholesale price — requiring Spin Master to staff a 200-person Toronto factory.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: A ~3x retail markup on a novelty item with ~57% supplier gross margin shows why retailers chase these SKUs — and why supply-chain readiness, not demand, is the usual failure point.
insights.quote: I'm going to order 48,000 pieces from you, and if it goes well, I'm going to order half a million pieces for Christmas.

insights.claim: Harary's model of novelty products is that they carry 'peak magic' consumable in one or two experiences, after which demand collapses — and that high sales velocity accelerates the collapse because it lets the entire addressable audience experience the product at once.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive: for fad-driven consumer names, a blowout quarter is evidence of a nearer-term demand cliff, not a durable trend — extrapolating run-rates is the classic error.
insights.quote: novelty products are something you want to experience once or twice and then once you've experienced it you want to move on to something else

insights.claim: Harary attributes the devil sticks success — 1.5 million units at $14.99 — primarily to timing rather than product attributes, noting quality, price and design were good but 'the moment' did the selling.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Assigns the variance in fad outcomes to exogenous cultural timing, implying these revenue streams should be valued at low multiples regardless of execution quality.
insights.quote: what really sold it was the moment more than anything else

insights.claim: Harary's trend-detection signal for devil sticks was demographic anomaly — the product was known to him as a late-teen/hippie item from Grateful Dead shows, so ten-year-olds hand-making them in schoolyards indicated an emerging shift in the kids' market.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: A transferable scouting rule: watch for a product migrating outside its native demographic, especially into unmonetized DIY form, as the earliest adoption signal.

insights.claim: Spin Master actively tried to amplify the devil sticks fad with vans, hired college students touring campus to campus doing tricks, a first TV commercial and heavy PR — what Harary calls the 1990s version of earned media — because they had little advertising budget.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that fad velocity is partially manufacturable through demonstration-based earned media, a low-capex playbook still used for viral consumer products.

insights.claim: Air Hogs solved its critical failure mode — wings snapping on landing — not by making wings stronger but by engineering them to pop off on impact and be reattached, and the product generated $35 million in its first nine months.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: A durable product-design principle with hard revenue attached: designing the failure mode to be cheap and reversible beats trying to eliminate it.

insights.claim: Russ Roberts maps the pop-off wing directly onto Arnold Kling's post-2008 argument that policy should aim to reduce the cost of financial crises rather than prevent them, since suppressed crises return larger.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts
insights.so_what: Applies a systems-resilience lens to macro policy and portfolio construction: build for graceful degradation and recovery cost, not for zero drawdowns.
insights.quote: So instead of trying to prevent it from happening, try to reduce the cost of when it happens.

insights.claim: Harary's central escape from the novelty half-life problem is attaching a narrative universe to a physical toy, because a TV-show character carries emotional resonance that turns a repeat play action from a diminishing visual novelty into an ongoing story the child inhabits.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: The core value-creation mechanism in toys: content converts a one-shot novelty cash flow into a multi-year annuity, which is why IP ownership dominates product design in this sector.

insights.claim: Harary declined the Beyblade license from Takara Tomy in 2001; it went on to become a multi-billion-dollar franchise at Hasbro, and that miss became the explicit strategic mandate that produced Bakugan five years later.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: A documented case where a single passed deal reset a company's strategy; the toy-plus-anime battling format was demonstrably replicable rather than a one-off.

insights.claim: Bakugan originated as a 23-year-old outside inventor's concept of an action figure inside a marble that Spin Master licensed and only partially developed; Sega Toys in Japan added the pop-open transformation and laminated metal card after Tomy and Bandai both turned the pitch down.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Shows the value stack in toys is distributed across licensor, mechanism engineer and marketer — and that two of the three largest Japanese incumbents misjudged a franchise that reached roughly a billion units.

insights.claim: Harary committed to a 52-episode Bakugan animated series after Sega Toys' Koko Bunan quoted $12 million and asked Spin Master to fund half, a decision Harary had to take back to his partners.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Prices the entry ticket to the narrative flywheel: roughly $6M of co-funded content unlocked a franchise Harary estimates at about a billion units produced.
insights.quote: It's going to cost $12 million. Do you have six?

insights.claim: Harary's evidence that narrative IP creates durable, non-novelty attachment is a 22-year-old South African tennis pro who still kept 25 mint-condition Bakugan from age eight — leading Harary to conclude the company created the product but the customer lived it.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Retained emotional attachment 14 years after purchase is the qualitative basis for reboot and nostalgia-cycle economics in toy and entertainment IP.
insights.quote: we created Bakugan but this kid lived it

insights.claim: Paw Patrol is in its 13th year producing 52 episodes annually plus specials, with a third movie dated August 14, and Harary estimates roughly 250 million children have been touched by it — a scale Roberts contrasts with about 600 million Harry Potter books sold.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Establishes preschool IP as a reach category comparable to the largest publishing franchises, with a far more repeatable annual content cadence.

insights.claim: Preschool IP escapes the jump-the-shark decay that afflicts adult streaming series because the audience fully replenishes every few years, removing the pressure to escalate plot novelty that degrades long-running shows.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts and Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: A structural argument that preschool franchises have longer, lower-risk IP duration than adult episodic content — relevant to how streaming and toy IP libraries should be valued.

insights.claim: Harary enforces hard creative boundaries — Paw Patrol will never go to space — and keeps the three-act episode structure, pacing, comedy and tone invariant while varying only the surface setting, a discipline he likens to keeping a song's melody fixed while jamming around it.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: A concrete operating rule for IP stewardship: constrain the format, vary the skin — the opposite of the escalation instinct that kills long-running franchises.
insights.quote: Paw Patrol will never go to space because that's just not that's just too far too far a field

insights.claim: Paw Patrol's development method physically co-located toy designers with animators and writers so they drew over each other's work, importing a practice from Bakugan that Harary says no one had done in North America.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Explains why toy-first companies can out-execute studios on merchandisable IP: play pattern and story are designed jointly rather than licensed sequentially.

insights.claim: Paw Patrol came from a structured brief sent to five creators worldwide asking for a transformation concept for preschoolers, was won by Bob the Builder creator Keith Chapman, and hit in Spin Master's 19th year in the toy business.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: The company's largest franchise came from a commissioned competitive brief 19 years in — evidence that hit IP is a sourcing-process output, not a founding-moment accident.

insights.claim: Harary claims he has never cancelled a standing weekly meeting in his career and argues the low-pressure sessions with nothing on the agenda are precisely where the best ideas emerge.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Directly against the efficiency-driven consensus to cancel agenda-less meetings; treats recurring unstructured contact as the generative asset.
insights.quote: I never cancel a meeting ever. I've never canceled a meeting, okay, in my whole career

insights.claim: Harary runs meetings as real-time expanding jam sessions — historically paging colleagues over the intercom mid-meeting so a two-person conversation could grow to eight or nine — and deliberately refuses to end a productive meeting on schedule.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: An operating model built around capturing inspiration at the moment it appears rather than scheduling it, with an explicit tradeoff of organizational disruption.
insights.quote: It's actually the meetings it's the meetings that you actually have less to talk about with less pressure that the good ideas start to come out.

insights.claim: Harary says Spin Master promotes on quality of thinking rather than function or credential, citing a known path from the shipping department to senior vice president, and deliberately draws out introverts because they hold the highest-value unspoken insights.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: A talent-allocation model that treats diversity of thought as the scarce input in a hit-driven creative business.
insights.quote: you can start in shipping and you you can, it's famous, you'll end up being a senior vice president at our company

themes.theme: Business as Creative Act and Founder Succession

insights.claim: Harary argues business is materially identical to art — the medium is coordinated human beings rather than paint — and that its poor cultural reputation comes from conflating profit motive with the creative act of bringing something new into existence.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Roberts adds the sharper point that observers assume money is the motive when it is the vehicle — a persistent misread of founder behavior in valuation and governance debates.
insights.quote: instead of using um paints, it's human beings coming together in a coordinated fashion to create something that's never been done before

insights.claim: Harary treats Hatchimals — the 2016 heat-activated hatching-egg toy that became highly successful while he was co-CEO and still involved in product but had zero involvement in — as the proof point that Spin Master's creative culture had become self-replicating.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: A concrete, testable succession metric for founder-led creative companies: hits produced without founder involvement, which Harary rates above any single product's economics.
insights.quote: if the company, God willing, could live beyond the founders, that's the highest form of success

insights.claim: Harary argues play patterns are eternal while only the enabling technology changes, citing that pull-string plush mechanics from the 1950s persist in products sold today.
insights.speaker: Ronnen Harary
insights.so_what: Implies the durable asset in toys is the play mechanic and the IP wrapped around it, not the technology layer — a reason to discount technology-novelty-driven toy theses.
insights.quote: the play patterns are actually eternal. They're just the technologies just change
